Explanation: All four are phase II conjugation reactions that attach an endogenous polar group (glucuronic acid, acetyl, sulfate, or methyl) to a substrate; conjugation increases polarity but does not invariably inactivate the drug.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Phase II metabolism; Drug conjugation reactions
Notes: Verified canonical phase II conjugations (Okunlola & Aleku, Angew Chem Int Ed 2026; Truong et al., J Med Food 2021; Moyer & Reid, Yamada's Textbook of Gastroenterology 7e 2022). Glutathione and amino-acid conjugation are other valid members; a 5th-member board tile could blur this category.

Explanation: Each induces hepatic CYP enzymes and can lower exposure to susceptible active-drug substrates; affected isoenzymes and magnitude differ by drug and substrate.
Notes: All four verified as classic CYP inducers across CYP3A4/2C9/2C19 (Camilleri, Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol 2019, Table 2; Song et al., Clin Pharmacokinet 2021, Table 1). BOARD OVERLAP: carbamazepine, phenobarbital, phenytoin also fit an antiseizure-drug category; rifampin does not. Do not imply identical isoenzyme specificity.

Explanation: Each inhibits one or more CYP enzymes and can raise exposure to susceptible substrates; the predominant enzyme differs among them.
Notes: Verified: clarithromycin and ritonavir are potent CYP3A4 inhibitors (ritonavir also used as a PK booster); amiodarone inhibits CYP2C9/2D6; cimetidine is a weaker multi-CYP/2D6 inhibitor (Camilleri 2019 Table 2; Song et al. 2021 Table 1). Keep the one-or-more-enzymes wording given cimetidine is comparatively weak.

Explanation: Each couples preferentially to Gq/11, activating phospholipase C-beta to generate IP3 and DAG and raise intracellular calcium.
Source Section: Autonomic System > Autonomic Secondary Messengers and Other Involuntary Signaling Systems, pp. 25, 27
Notes: Verified: M1/M3 (and M5) couple to Gq/11 (Nelic et al., Sci Rep 2024); alpha-1 to Gq (Insel, NEJM 1996); H1 is Gq-coupled (standard pharmacology). Coupling is preferential not exclusive. Other Gq members: AT1, V1, 5-HT2.

Explanation: Each couples preferentially to Gs, stimulating adenylyl cyclase and raising cAMP.
Source Section: Autonomic System > Autonomic Secondary Messengers and Other Involuntary Signaling Systems, pp. 25, 27
Notes: Verified: beta-adrenergic receptors couple to Gs (Insel, NEJM 1996); D1/D5 to Gs-alpha (Sidhu, Mol Neurobiol 1998; Goldstein & Eisenhofer, Physiol Rev 2026); V2 is Gs-coupled (standard pharmacology). BOARD OVERLAP: beta-1/beta-2 also fit an adrenergic-receptor category. Other Gs members: H2, 5-HT4, D5.

Explanation: Each directly stimulates muscarinic acetylcholine receptors; target organs and uses differ (sicca/xerostomia, urinary or GI atony, bronchoprovocation testing).
Source Section: Autonomic System > Cholinomimetics - Direct Agonists, p. 28
Notes: Verified: pilocarpine and cevimeline are direct muscarinic M1/M3 agonists (Farag et al., Oral Dis 2019; Hosseini et al., Eur J Med Res 2024); bethanechol and methacholine are direct choline esters (Finkbeiner et al., Urology 1977). Carbachol is another valid member (board note).

Explanation: All four inhibit acetylcholinesterase and cross the blood-brain barrier; the first three are used in Alzheimer disease, whereas physostigmine (a tertiary amine) is used in antimuscarinic (anticholinergic) toxicity.
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Centrally acting AChE inhibitors; BBB-penetrating AChE inhibitors
Notes: Central activity of donepezil/rivastigmine/galantamine verified (Li et al., Cochrane 2015; Noetzli & Eap, Clin Pharmacokinet 2013; Mayeux & Sano, NEJM 1999). Physostigmine is a tertiary amine that crosses the BBB, unlike quaternary neostigmine/pyridostigmine (standard pharmacology). Do not label all four as Alzheimer treatments.

Connection Title: Peripheral muscarinic findings in organophosphate (cholinergic) poisoning
Explanation: Excess acetylcholine at peripheral muscarinic receptors produces these findings; nicotinic effects (fasciculations, weakness) and central effects (seizures) are separate categories.
Notes: Verified muscarinic toxidrome features (Roberts et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2026; Henretig et al., NEJM 2019; Lavonas et al., AHA 2023; Cao et al., AHA 2025). Direct muscarinic-agonist excess reproduces the same quartet, so a general muscarinic-toxicity label is accepted. BOARD OVERLAP: each sign individually appears in other toxidromes.

Explanation: Muscarinic blockade produces dilated pupils, decreased sweating, impaired bladder emptying, and increased heart rate.
Source Section: Autonomic System > Muscarinic Antagonists > Atropine Poisoning, p. 31
Notes: Verified antimuscarinic toxidrome (Roberts et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2026, Fig 6). Dry skin/anhidrosis distinguishes anticholinergic from sympathomimetic toxicity (diaphoresis). BOARD OVERLAP: mydriasis and tachycardia also occur in sympathomimetic toxicity.

Explanation: Each is a centrally acting alpha-2 agonist that reduces sympathetic outflow or alters central transmission; uses span hypertension, ADHD, sedation, and spasticity.
Notes: Verified: clonidine, guanfacine, dexmedetomidine are central alpha-2 agonists (Chen et al., Cochrane 2015; Duncan et al., Cochrane 2018; Lee et al., Clin Drug Investig 2025); tizanidine is a central alpha-2 agonist (FDA Zanaflex label; Coward, Neurology 1994, PMID 7970012). Methyldopa is another member. Do not imply shared indications.

Explanation: Each blocks alpha-1 receptors; tamsulosin is relatively uroselective (alpha-1A), while the others have more prominent vascular effects.
Source Section: Autonomic System > Alpha Adrenergic Antagonists, p. 37
Notes: Verified alpha-1 antagonist class (standard pharmacology; FDA labels). Alfuzosin and silodosin are other members (board note). Avoid a shared BPH-treatment category because prazosin is not a standard contemporary BPH agent.

Explanation: Each preferentially antagonizes beta-1 receptors; selectivity is relative and decreases at higher doses.
Source Section: Autonomic System > Beta Adrenergic Antagonists, p. 38
Notes: Verified second-generation cardioselective beta-blockers (Safi et al., Cochrane 2019/2021; Triposkiadis et al., JACC 2009). Cardioselectivity is dose-dependent. Acebutolol, betaxolol, nebivolol are other members. Do not imply chronic HFrEF survival benefit for esmolol or atenolol.

Connection Title: Nonselective beta blockers without alpha blockade
Explanation: Each antagonizes beta-1 and beta-2 without the alpha-1 blockade of carvedilol or labetalol; sotalol additionally blocks potassium channels (class III).
Accepted Alternate Category Names: Nonselective beta antagonists; Beta-1 and beta-2 blockers
Source Section: Autonomic System > Beta Adrenergic Antagonists, p. 38
Notes: Verified first-generation nonselective beta-blockers (Triposkiadis et al., JACC 2009; Safi et al., Cochrane 2019). BOARD OVERLAP: sotalol also fits class III antiarrhythmics; its added K-channel activity does not negate its beta-blockade. Pindolol and carteolol are other members.

Explanation: Each inhibits PDE-5, reducing cGMP breakdown and promoting smooth-muscle relaxation; clinical indications are not identical across the four.
Notes: Verified PDE-5 inhibitor class incl. avanafil (Elzupir & Almahmoud, PLoS One 2025; Samidurai et al., Annu Rev Pharmacol Toxicol 2023, PMID 36206989; Tzoumas et al., Br J Pharmacol 2020, PMID 31721165). Erectile-dysfunction and nitrate-incompatible labels name the SAME four drugs (accepted alternates); avoid duplicating this quartet on a board.

Explanation: Each activates cardiac beta-1 receptors and increases myocardial contractility, although vascular effects and reflex responses differ.
Source Section: Autonomic System > Endogenous Adrenergic Agonists, Direct Sympathomimetics and Physiological Effects, pp. 32-35
Notes: Verified beta-1 inotropic activity for all four (Bjorklund et al., Pediatr Rev 2023, vasoactive spectrum). Norepinephrine can cause reflex bradycardia despite direct beta-1 inotropy; do not title this group as drugs that always raise heart rate.

Connection Title: Toxic exposures treated with chelation therapy
Explanation: Each toxicity is managed with a chelating agent; agent choice depends on the metal, chemical form, and acuity (dimercaprol/DMSA/EDTA for lead; DMSA/DMPS for mercury and arsenic; deferoxamine/deferasirox for iron).
Source Section: Side Effects and Toxins > Environmental Toxins and their Treatments, p. 46
Notes: Verified chelation-treatment relationship (Bjorklund et al., Arch Toxicol 2017, PMID 29063135; Balali-Mood et al., Heliyon 2025, PMID 40040983; Vellingiri et al., J Neurol 2022). This is a treatment category, not a strict heavy-metal chemical class (iron is treated with deferoxamine, not dimercaprol). Copper (penicillamine) is another valid member; set is not exhaustive.
